clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, asthma, and respiratory reactions to aspirin and other cyclo-oxygenase-1 inhibiting NSAIDs
Reactions typically manifest as bronchospasm, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion and sometimes ocular or cutaneous symptoms within one to three hours of NSAID exposure
The nasal polyps tend to be extensive and recur rapidly after surgery, and the asthma is often difficult to control
It is a non-IgE-mediated pseudo-allergy, so conventional allergy skin testing to aspirin is not diagnostic
Anosmia or marked hyposmia is common and often an early feature
Diagnosis is clinical, supported where needed by supervised aspirin provocation challenge in an appropriate setting
Management combines control of sinonasal and asthmatic inflammation, strict NSAID avoidance, and consideration of aspirin desensitisation in selected patients
Leukotriene-modifying drugs and biologic therapies targeting type 2 inflammation are useful adjuncts
reference.pathophysiology: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease is driven by dysregulation of arachidonic acid metabolism in a background of chronic eosinophilic type 2 airway inflammation. Affected individuals have constitutively increased production of pro-inflammatory cysteinyl leukotrienes and relatively deficient protective prostaglandin E2 signalling. Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase-1 by aspirin or other NSAIDs removes the restraining influence of prostaglandin E2, causing a surge in cysteinyl leukotrienes that provokes bronchoconstriction and nasosinusal inflammation. The same underlying eosinophilic inflammation produces the recalcitrant nasal polyposis and asthma even in the absence of NSAID exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps without aspirin sensitivity
Cystic fibrosis with sinonasal polyps in younger patients
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to assess polyp burden and distribution
CT of the paranasal sinuses to define disease extent before surgery
Pulmonary function testing to characterise and monitor asthma
Supervised graded aspirin provocation challenge where the diagnosis is uncertain
Blood and tissue eosinophil assessment to gauge type 2 inflammation
redFlags: Severe bronchospasm or anaphylactoid reaction after NSAID ingestion
Acute severe asthma exacerbation with respiratory compromise
Rapidly recurring or obstructive polyps threatening the airway or vision
Features suggesting vasculitis such as neuropathy, purpura or systemic involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition is chronic and tends to relapse, with nasal polyps frequently recurring after surgery and asthma often persistent. Multimodal management including NSAID avoidance, aspirin desensitisation in suitable patients, leukotriene modifiers and biologic therapy can substantially improve symptom control and quality of life.
pitfalls: Giving aspirin or NSAIDs for unrelated indications and precipitating a severe reaction
Relying on conventional allergy testing, which does not detect this pseudo-allergic mechanism
Repeated polyp surgery without addressing the underlying inflammatory drive
Overlooking eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis in patients with systemic features
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Strict avoidance of aspirin and other cyclo-oxygenase-1-inhibiting NSAIDs as the central trigger, with education on hidden sources
Leukotriene-modifying therapy with a leukotriene receptor antagonist or 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor to counter the excess cysteinyl leukotrienes
Intranasal corticosteroids and saline irrigation for the nasal polyposis, with inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators for the asthma
Aspirin desensitisation followed by maintenance aspirin therapy in suitable patients to reduce polyp recurrence and improve control
Biologic therapy targeting type 2 inflammation, such as anti-interleukin-5, anti-interleukin-4/13 or anti-IgE agents, for refractory disease
Endoscopic sinus surgery to debulk extensive polyps, recognising the high rate of recurrence
Monitoring with serial pulmonary function testing and nasal endoscopy through a joint otolaryngology, allergy and respiratory service
